final_answer:
A hash table handles collisions by employing methods to resolve conflicts when two keys hash to the same index. The two primary approaches are chaining and open addressing. 

Chaining involves storing a linked list (or another data structure) at each bucket of the hash table. When a collision occurs, the new element is added to the linked list at that bucket. Chaining is simple to implement and allows efficient insertion and deletion. However, performance degrades if too many elements hash to the same bucket, increasing search times.

Open addressing involves finding an alternative bucket within the hash table itself when a collision occurs. Techniques like linear probing, quadratic probing, and double hashing are used. Open addressing can be more cache-friendly since all elements are stored in the table. However, it can be more complex to implement and may lead to clustering issues, which can degrade performance.

In terms of trade-offs, chaining tends to perform better with high collision rates, while open addressing may be more efficient in memory usage and cache performance. The choice depends on the specific requirements of the application.
